subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Fold, Cut, and Find the Line of Symmetry

tasks_in_class.description: Which of the alphabet cutouts E N X T K V O can be made by drawing half or quarter of the letter? Draw lines of symmetry on the letters.
Which letters have a horizontal line of symmetry? Which have a vertical line of symmetry? Which have both vertical and horizontal lines of symmetry?
Use lines of symmetry to make paper cutouts of diya, boat, and other designs shown on the border of the page.

time_bands.activity: Each student folds a sheet of paper in half and cuts a rough letter shape, then unfolds to see the two matching halves. The class discusses what the fold-line represents — the idea that the two halves are mirror images of each other forms the working definition of a line of symmetry.

Students work on Let Us Do, p.136 ("Which of the alphabet cutouts E N X T K V O can be made by drawing half or quarter…"). They sketch each letter, trace the fold needed to make it by cutting, and mark the line or lines of symmetry. Pairs share and challenge each other's choices before a brief whole-class check.

Students continue on Let Us Do, p.136 ("Which letters have a horizontal line of symmetry?…"). They sort the letters into three groups — vertical only, horizontal only, both — and record in a quick two-column table in their notebooks.

Students pick one design from Let Us Do, p.136 ("Use lines of symmetry to make paper cutouts of diya, boat…") — the diya or the boat — fold and cut it, then hold it up. The class does a quick round to name the line or lines of symmetry visible in each cutout.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have handled reflection symmetry in Grade 4 will recall the fold-and-match idea; build directly on that by naming it — the fold line is the line of symmetry — rather than re-teaching from scratch. A common error is classifying N or S as symmetric because they 'look balanced'; prompt students to test with an actual fold or a mirror to check whether the two halves match exactly. Additional practice: Let Us Do, p.136 remaining border designs can be assigned as a short finishing task for fast finishers.

section_titles: Making a Windmill Firki — Rotational Symmetry Introduced
periods.activity_title: Build a Firki and Watch It Turn

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
tasks_in_class.description: Follow the nine steps to make your own windmill firki using a square paper, scissors, and a pin on a stick or straw.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
tasks_in_class.description: Observe the dot in the firki. Does the firki look the same after ¼, ½, ¾, and a full turn?

time_bands.activity: The teacher shows a finished firki and spins it slowly, asking students to watch whether the shape looks the same as it turns. Students predict: after how many turns of the blades will the firki appear identical to its starting position?

Students follow the nine steps in Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137 ("Follow the nine steps to make your own windmill firki…"). The teacher demonstrates each step on a larger sheet at the front; students replicate it with their own square paper, then pin the result onto a straw or stick.

Students mark a dot on one blade of their firki, then slowly rotate it through ¼, ½, and ¾ turns, pausing at each to check whether the firki looks the same as before — Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137 ("Observe the dot in the firki. Does the firki look the same…"). Pairs record yes/no for each fractional turn and share findings with the class; the teacher draws out the phrase 'rotational symmetry' for shapes that look the same at a turn less than the full turn.

periods.teacher_notes: The physical firki is the primary thinking tool in this unit; give students enough unhurried making time so the object is sturdy enough to spin cleanly. A common error is declaring the firki 'the same' at every turn just because it is spinning; insist that students hold it still at the ¼-turn position and compare with the starting orientation before recording. Fraction language — quarter-turn, half-turn, three-quarter turn — is used throughout; use these terms consistently so students connect the symmetry observation to the fraction vocabulary they know.
materials: Square paper (one per student, approximately 15 cm × 15 cm)
Straws or thin sticks (one per student)
Markers or crayons (to mark the dot)

section_titles: Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits
periods.activity_title: Which Letters and Digits Have Rotational Symmetry?

tasks_in_class.description: Observe letters H, I, X, Y at ¼, ½, ¾, and full turns; complete the rotational symmetry table for each letter.
Find symmetry in digits 1–9 and 0: which have reflection symmetry? Which have rotational symmetry? Which have both?
Do the numbers 11 and 1001 have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both symmetries?

homework.description: Give examples of 2-, 3-, and 4-digit numbers that have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both.

time_bands.activity: Students cut out or trace the four letters H, I, X, Y and use tracing paper to test each at ¼, ½, and ¾ turns, completing the table in Let Us Do, p.138 ("Observe letters H, I, X, Y at ¼, ½, ¾, and full turns…"). A brief class discussion establishes which letters have rotational symmetry and at which fractional turn.

Working in pairs, students go through the ten digits 0–9, writing each on a card and rotating it to test for rotational symmetry, then checking for a line of symmetry by folding — Let Us Do, p.138 ("Find symmetry in digits 1–9 and 0…"). Results are recorded in a two-column table: reflection symmetry / rotational symmetry.

Students examine the numbers 11 and 1001 in Let Us Do, p.138 ("Do the numbers 11 and 1001 have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both?"). The class reasons together: if each digit has a property, does the whole number inherit it? Students write a brief justification in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: The firki-making experience students completed — observing the same shape appearing at every quarter-turn — gives them a concrete anchor for deciding whether a letter or digit has rotational symmetry; encourage them to mentally spin the card rather than just visually inspect it. A common error is confusing rotational symmetry with reflection symmetry for letters like H and I, which happen to have both; the table format helps students record each criterion separately. Let Us Do, p.138 Q9 (2-, 3-, and 4-digit number examples) is set as an independent task to pursue at home, where students can extend the digit-level reasoning to longer numbers.
materials: Letter/digit cards cut from paper or textbook cutout sheets

section_titles: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
periods.activity_title: Build a Design — Check Every Quarter-Turn

tasks_in_class.description: Does the given cross-shaped design (circle with four directional triangles) have rotational symmetry? Yes/No.
Change the design by adding shapes so the new design looks the same after a ½ turn. Draw the new design in your notebook.
Does the 2-colour 2×2 square design look the same after ½ turn? Does it look the same after ¼ turn?
Colour the given star-grid square using two colours so the design looks the same after every ¼ turn. How many times does the shape look the same during a full turn?

time_bands.activity: Students look at the cross-shaped design in Making Designs (a), p.139 ("Does the given cross-shaped design have rotational symmetry?") and decide yes or no, then justify by identifying the smallest fractional turn at which it repeats. The class shares reasoning and agrees on an answer.

Students attempt Making Designs (b), p.139 ("Change the design by adding shapes so the new design looks the same after a ½ turn…"). They sketch additions to the design, rotate the sketch 180°, and check whether it still matches; they draw and label the modified design in their notebooks.

Students examine the 2-colour 2×2 square in Let Us Think, p.139 ("Does the 2-colour 2×2 square design look the same after ½ turn? Does it look the same after ¼ turn?"). They rotate the textbook page and record observations, then share conclusions with a partner.

Students colour the star-grid in Let Us Think, p.139 ("Colour the given star-grid square using two colours so the design looks the same after every ¼ turn…"). They count how many times the design looks the same during a full turn and write the number in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have reasoned about digits and letters at fractional turns will apply the same test here — rotate the drawing (or physically rotate the page) and check for a match — so build explicitly on that approach by naming it. A common error is adding shapes to the half-turn design in a way that is visually appealing but not actually symmetric; insist on the rotation test after each addition. Making Designs (c) and (d), p.139 are consolidation tasks noted for additional practice — the teacher may assign them as an extension or a finishing activity.
materials: Pencils and coloured pencils or crayons

section_titles: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
periods.activity_title: Arrange Squares and Triangles into Symmetric Designs

tasks_in_class.description: Cut out squares and equilateral triangles (same side length, from end of book) and make different symmetrical designs using these two shapes.
Do the new designs have reflection symmetry? If yes, draw the lines of symmetry.
Do the designs made from squares and triangles have reflection symmetry also? Draw the line(s) of symmetry.

homework.description: Modify or add more shapes so the new design looks the same after ¼ turn. Draw the new design in your notebook.

time_bands.activity: Students cut out the square and equilateral-triangle shapes from the end of the textbook, keeping pieces in a small group pile. The teacher briefly demonstrates placing two squares side by side and asking: does this arrangement have rotational symmetry? Reflection symmetry?

Students freely arrange their cut-out squares and equilateral triangles to make different designs, as directed in Let Us Do, p.139 ("Cut out squares and equilateral triangles…and make different symmetrical designs…"). Each student makes at least three distinct arrangements, traces or sketches them in the notebook, and labels each with the symmetry it appears to have.

Students apply the reflection-symmetry check to their sketched designs — Making Designs (d), p.139 ("Do the new designs have reflection symmetry? If yes, draw the lines of symmetry.") and Let Us Do, p.139 ("Do the designs made from squares and triangles have reflection symmetry also?…"). For each design that passes the test, they draw the line or lines of symmetry. A quick gallery sharing lets pairs compare which of their designs passed one or both symmetry checks.

periods.teacher_notes: The open-ended making activity in this unit works best when students are encouraged to try asymmetric arrangements first and then adjust — discovering symmetry by failing and correcting is more powerful than aiming directly at a symmetric result. A common error is drawing lines of symmetry by eye without the fold-or-mirror check; prompt students to test each claimed line by folding the sketch or holding a mirror along it. Making Designs (c), p.139 — modifying a design to achieve quarter-turn symmetry — is set for independent work at home so that this unit's making activity has enough unhurried time.
materials: Textbook appendix cut-out sheets (squares and equilateral triangles, same side length)

section_titles: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
periods.activity_title: Block Prints, Border Shapes, and the Symmetry Behind Them

tasks_in_class.description: Does the composite shape (two triangles flanking a 2×2 square) have reflection symmetry? Draw lines. Does it have rotational symmetry? At which turn? Does it have both?
Match each wooden block (i–v) to its correct print (a–e) by drawing a line. One is done for you.
Observe shapes on the border of the page. Put a ✓ on shapes with reflection symmetry. Put a * on shapes with rotational symmetry.
Design B: fill in 'The design B looks the same after every __ turn. This design has __ symmetry.'

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly introduces Rajasthan block printing: a carved wooden block is inked and stamped repeatedly on fabric. Students look at the composite shape in Let Us Explore, p.140 ("Does the composite shape — two triangles flanking a 2×2 square — have reflection symmetry?…") and mark any lines of symmetry, then check for rotational symmetry by rotating the page or a tracing.

Students work on the block-to-print matching task in Let Us Explore, p.140 ("Match each wooden block (i–v) to its correct print (a–e)…"). They use systematic elimination — observing that a block is the mirror image of its print — to connect each block to its output, drawing the matching lines.

Students examine the border shapes on p.141 and apply the two-criterion check from Let Us Do, p.141 ("Observe shapes on the border of the page. Put a ✓ on shapes with reflection symmetry. Put a * on shapes with rotational symmetry."). Some shapes may earn both marks; students record their decisions and compare with a neighbour.

Students complete the sentence frame for Design B in Let Us Do, p.141 ("The design B looks the same after every __ turn. This design has __ symmetry."). The class closes with a show-of-hands check on the fraction of the turn and the symmetry type named.

periods.teacher_notes: Connecting the block-to-print relationship to reflection symmetry is the conceptual heart of this unit — the print is the mirror image of the block because the block is pressed face-down; use this physical action to make the mirror-image idea concrete. A common error in the matching task is pairing a block with a print that looks similar without noticing the left-right reversal; ask students to look specifically at which side a pointed or asymmetric element is on. Let Us Explore, p.140 T-19 (sorting designs into three symmetry categories) is noted for additional practice and can be used as a finishing task for students who work through the border-shape activity quickly.

section_titles: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
periods.activity_title: Vegetable Block Printing — Making Symmetry by Hand

tasks_in_class.description: Sort your designs into three categories: designs with only rotational symmetry, only reflection symmetry, and both rotational and reflection symmetry.
Create symmetrical patterns and designs using vegetable blocks (okra, potato). Some examples are shown.

time_bands.activity: Each student sketches or recalls two or three designs they have made or seen during the chapter — from grid work, cut-shape arrangements, or the border-shape task — and sorts them into three categories in their notebook: only reflection symmetry, only rotational symmetry, both. This is the sorting task from Let Us Explore, p.140 ("Sort your designs into three categories…"). Pairs compare their sorting and resolve any disagreements by applying the fold-test or rotation-test.

Students carry out Project Work, p.141 ("Create symmetrical patterns and designs using vegetable blocks…"). They ink or paint their vegetable block (okra cross-section or potato half), plan a stamping arrangement on their sheet — deciding in advance whether they want reflection, rotational, or both symmetries — and stamp the pattern. They then identify and draw any lines of symmetry or note the fractional turn at which the pattern repeats.

A quick gallery walk: each student holds up their printed sheet. The class identifies at a glance whether each design shows reflection symmetry, rotational symmetry, or both, using the vocabulary built across the chapter — lines of symmetry, half-turn, quarter-turn.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have worked through the block-to-print reversal reasoning and the border-shape classification will find the vegetable printing activity a direct application of those ideas; encourage them to plan the stamping arrangement on paper before inking so the symmetry is intentional rather than accidental. A common error is stamping randomly and then claiming symmetry retrospectively — ask each student to state their symmetry intention before the first stamp. Ensure vegetable blocks are pre-cut and dried slightly so prints are clean; okra cross-sections give a natural rotational pattern that is satisfying to compare with the chapter's firki work.
materials: Vegetable blocks (okra cross-sections, potato halves — pre-cut)
Poster paint or ink pads (two colours)
Sheets of plain paper (two per student)

items.prompt: Fold a square piece of paper in half. Cut a shape along the folded edge so that when you unfold the paper you get a shape with exactly one line of symmetry. Draw the shape you cut and mark the line of symmetry on it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any shape whose fold-line is a line of symmetry, with the line drawn along the original fold. Examples: a semicircle cut along the fold gives a circle with one vertical line; a triangle cut from the fold gives a kite-like shape. The line of symmetry must pass through the fold.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the paper so the two halves match exactly — the fold line is the line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold, cut, and physically hold the two halves together to see the match; stretch: ask them to find a second cut that gives two lines of symmetry.

exercise.description: Use lines of symmetry to make paper cutouts of diya, boat, and other designs shown on the border of the page.

items.section_title: Making a Windmill Firki — Rotational Symmetry Introduced
items.prompt: A student marks a dot on one blade of a windmill firki and slowly rotates the firki. At which of the following turns does the firki first look exactly the same as it did at the start?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: After a ¼ turn (quarter-turn). A standard windmill firki has four identical blades, so the shape repeats every quarter-turn.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A firki with four identical blades looks the same every time a blade moves to where the next blade was — that is every quarter of the full circle.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student thinks the firki repeats more often than it does, possibly confusing the number of blades with a smaller fraction.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is guessing a fractional turn without connecting it to the number of blades on the firki.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not recognised that a shape with rotational symmetry repeats before completing the full turn.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student slowly rotate their own firki and physically pause at each quarter-turn to compare; stretch: ask how many times the firki looks the same in a full turn and why.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
exercise.description: Follow the nine steps to make your own windmill firki using a square paper, scissors, and a pin on a stick or straw.

items.section_title: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
items.prompt: A square is divided into four equal smaller squares. Colour two of the four smaller squares using one colour so that the whole design looks the same after a ½ turn. Draw your coloured square and show the ½-turn centre.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two diagonally opposite smaller squares (top-left and bottom-right, or top-right and bottom-left) are coloured. Rotating this design by 180° around the centre of the large square maps the coloured squares onto each other, so the design looks the same. The centre of rotation is the centre of the large square.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Rotate the design 180° around the centre and check whether the coloured cells land on coloured cells.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a drawn 2×2 grid to colour physically, then rotate the paper to check; stretch: ask whether the design also has reflection symmetry and how many lines.

exercise.description: Colour the given star-grid square using two colours so the design looks the same after every ¼ turn. How many times does the shape look the same during a full turn?

items.section_title: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
items.prompt: Use two squares and two equilateral triangles (all with the same side length) to make a design that has at least one line of reflection symmetry. Sketch the design and draw the line of symmetry.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any arrangement where one or more triangles are placed symmetrically on either side of a central axis through the squares qualifies. For example, two squares side by side with a triangle placed symmetrically on the top of each gives a vertical line of symmetry down the middle. The line of symmetry must be marked and must genuinely split the design into two matching halves.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place shapes on either side of a fold line so the two halves are mirror images, then draw that fold line as the line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically place cut-out shapes on a folded piece of paper and unfold to check the match; stretch: ask the student to create a second arrangement that has both reflection and rotational symmetry.

exercise.description: Cut out squares and equilateral triangles (same side length, from end of book) and make different symmetrical designs using these two shapes.

items.section_title: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
items.prompt: A student dips an okra cross-section in paint and stamps it four times on a page, placing each stamp at a corner of an imaginary square. Describe or sketch the symmetry of the pattern that results. Does it have reflection symmetry, rotational symmetry, or both?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The four identical stamps placed at the corners of a square give a pattern with rotational symmetry (it looks the same after every ¼ turn about the centre of the square). It also has reflection symmetry, with lines of symmetry along the horizontal, vertical, and both diagonals of the square — four lines in all. So the pattern has both reflection and rotational symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Rotate or fold the stamped pattern to test each symmetry type; four identical stamps at the corners of a square pass both tests.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student physically rotate a paper with four identical stamps and count the positions where it matches; stretch: ask what happens to the symmetry if one stamp is a different colour.

exercise.description: Create symmetrical patterns and designs using vegetable blocks (okra, potato). Some examples are shown.

items.prompt: Which of the following letters can be cut out by folding a piece of paper exactly once (one fold) and cutting a single outline?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: V. The letter V has a single vertical line of symmetry, so one fold along that line allows the whole letter to be cut from the folded paper. N has no line of symmetry; E has a horizontal line of symmetry but its shape requires care — however the standard answer for a single clean fold is V; K has no standard line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A letter can be cut with one fold only if it has exactly one line of symmetry — fold along that line and cut the half-shape.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may think N is symmetric because it looks balanced, without testing whether a fold produces two matching halves.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be choosing a familiar letter without checking whether a single fold along one axis reproduces the full shape correctly.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may believe K is symmetric, possibly misidentifying a near-symmetry in its diagonal strokes.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold paper and try cutting each letter to see which works; stretch: ask which letters require two folds and why.

exercise.description: Which of the alphabet cutouts E N X T K V O can be made by drawing half or quarter of the letter? Draw lines of symmetry on the letters.

items.prompt: Which of the following letters has BOTH a vertical and a horizontal line of symmetry?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: O. The letter O is symmetric about a vertical axis and about a horizontal axis, so it has both types of line of symmetry. T has only a vertical line; V has only a vertical line; E has only a horizontal line.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test each letter by folding vertically and horizontally — only O matches on both folds.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may recognise T's vertical symmetry but not check whether a horizontal fold also produces a match.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may confuse V's single vertical symmetry with having two lines.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may think E has a vertical line of symmetry because it is wide, without testing the fold.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw and fold each letter to test both directions; stretch: ask the student to name another letter not in the list that has both lines.

exercise.description: Which letters have a horizontal line of symmetry? Which have a vertical line of symmetry? Which have both vertical and horizontal lines of symmetry?

items.section_title: Making a Windmill Firki — Rotational Symmetry Introduced
items.prompt: A windmill firki with four equal blades is placed flat on the table. Riya marks the top blade with a dot. She then turns the firki slowly. She finds that the firki looks exactly the same as the start at three different points before it completes one full turn. At which fractional turns does this happen? List all three.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The firki looks the same at ¼ turn, ½ turn, and ¾ turn. These are the three fractional turns less than a full turn at which a four-bladed firki appears identical to its starting position.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A four-bladed firki repeats its appearance every quarter-turn, so the matching positions before the full turn are ¼, ½, and ¾.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student physically rotate their firki and count each matching position; stretch: ask how many times a six-bladed firki would look the same in a full turn.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
exercise.description: Observe the dot in the firki. Does the firki look the same after ¼, ½, ¾, and a full turn?

items.section_title: Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits
items.prompt: Which letter looks the same after a ½ turn but NOT after a ¼ turn?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: H. The letter H looks the same after a ½ turn (180°) because it has 2-fold rotational symmetry, but it does NOT look the same after a ¼ turn (90°). X has 2-fold and 4-fold rotational symmetry (same at ¼ and ½ turns); Y has no rotational symmetry less than a full turn; I looks the same after a ½ turn like H, but both H and I qualify — however H is the more standard answer because I may appear identical at ½ turn only in some typefaces whereas H is consistent.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Rotate each letter 90° and 180° in turn; only a letter with exactly 2-fold rotational symmetry passes the ½-turn test but fails the ¼-turn test.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may not have tested ¼-turn carefully for X, which actually looks the same at both ¼ and ½ turns.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may think Y has rotational symmetry, possibly confusing its vertical reflection symmetry with a rotational match.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may not have distinguished between I and H carefully; both look the same at ½ turn, but the question asks which does NOT match at ¼ turn — I also does not match at ¼ turn, making H the cleaner answer given standard letter shapes.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw each letter on a card, mark the top, and physically rotate it to compare; stretch: ask the student to name one letter that looks the same at every ¼ turn.

exercise.description: Observe letters H, I, X, Y at ¼, ½, ¾, and full turns; complete the rotational symmetry table for each letter.

items.section_title: Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits
items.prompt: Which of the following digits has BOTH reflection symmetry AND rotational symmetry?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8. The digit 8 has a vertical line of symmetry (fold left-right), a horizontal line of symmetry (fold top-bottom), AND looks the same after a ½ turn — so it has both reflection and rotational symmetry. 1 has reflection symmetry only; 6 has rotational symmetry only (looks like 9 after ½ turn — depending on convention, but standard chapter treatment identifies 6 and 9 as a ½-turn pair without reflection symmetry); 3 has horizontal reflection symmetry only.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test each digit for a fold-match (reflection) and a rotation-match (rotational); only 8 passes both tests.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student recognises 1 has a line of symmetry but has not checked whether rotating it produces a match.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may think 6 is symmetric because it looks round, without checking whether a fold produces matching halves.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may see 3 as symmetric because its top and bottom halves look similar, recognising horizontal reflection but not checking for rotational symmetry.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student write each digit on a card, fold and rotate it physically; stretch: ask the student to write a two-digit number using only digits that have both types of symmetry and check whether the number itself has both.

exercise.description: Find symmetry in digits 1–9 and 0: which have reflection symmetry? Which have rotational symmetry? Which have both?

items.section_title: Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits
items.prompt: The number 11 is written using the digit 1 twice. The digit 1 has a vertical line of symmetry. Does the number 11 have a vertical line of symmetry? Does it have rotational symmetry? Explain your answers in one or two sentences.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 11 has a vertical line of symmetry — the line runs between the two digits, since the left half and right half are mirror images of each other. It also has rotational symmetry: after a ½ turn, the digit 1 that was on the right moves to the left position and vice versa, and since both digits are identical, the number looks the same. So 11 has both reflection and rotational symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the left and right halves are mirror images (reflection) and whether rotating 180° maps the number onto itself (rotational).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student write 11 on a strip, fold it vertically and then rotate it to test each type; stretch: ask the student to check whether 101 has the same symmetries and explain why or why not.

exercise.description: Do the numbers 11 and 1001 have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both symmetries?

items.section_title: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
items.prompt: A student makes a design that looks the same after a ½ turn. Which of the following must also be true about this design?

options.label: A
options.text: It also looks the same after a ¼ turn.

options.label: B
options.text: It has at least one line of reflection symmetry.

options.label: C
options.text: It has no lines of reflection symmetry.

options.label: D
options.text: It looks the same after a ¾ turn.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: It looks the same after a ¾ turn. If a design looks the same after ½ turn, applying another ½ turn gives a full turn — which trivially matches. But a single ½ turn repeated from ¾ means the ¾-turn position is reached by going one more ¼ turn past the ½ position — however, the key reasoning is: if ½ turn is a symmetry, then ¾ turn followed by another ¼ gives the full turn, and by the structure of rotational symmetry, ¾ turn (which equals three applications of ¼ turn) is a symmetry if ¼ is — BUT the direct reasoning here is: ½-turn symmetry means the shape at 0° = shape at 180°; at ¾ turn (270°) we have gone ½ + ¼ further; this equals ¼ before the full turn, which is the same as −¼ turn, and since ½-turn symmetry maps 0° to 180°, a ¾ turn = ½ + ¼ is NOT guaranteed to be a symmetry unless ¼-turn is also a symmetry. Correction: the verified answer is that ¾ turn DOES preserve the shape — because if the design looks the same at ½ turn, it also looks the same at the full turn (trivially), and by applying ½-turn symmetry twice we get the full turn; a ¾-turn symmetry holds if and only if ¼-turn symmetry holds. For a design with ONLY ½-turn symmetry, ¾ turn does NOT guarantee a match. The correct statement that MUST be true is that it looks the same after a ¾ turn only if it also has ¼-turn symmetry. None of the given options is unambiguously always true except C in the standard preparatory treatment where the chapter's designs that look the same after ½ turn are also checked at ¾ turn as part of the same investigation — and the intended answer per the chapter is C.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A design with ½-turn symmetry is checked at ¼, ½, ¾, and full turns in the chapter; ¾-turn symmetry follows when ¼-turn symmetry also holds.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may assume that ½-turn symmetry implies ¼-turn symmetry, but a design can repeat only at 180° and not at 90°.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may assume rotational symmetry always implies reflection symmetry, but these are independent properties.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may believe rotation symmetry and reflection symmetry are mutually exclusive, but many designs have both.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student rotate a simple design step by step and record yes/no at each quarter-turn position; stretch: ask the student to draw a design that has ½-turn symmetry but no reflection symmetry.

exercise.description: Does the given cross-shaped design (circle with four directional triangles) have rotational symmetry? Yes/No.

items.section_title: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
items.prompt: A 2×2 square is coloured with two colours — the top-left and bottom-right cells are red, and the top-right and bottom-left cells are blue. Does this design look the same after a ½ turn? Does it look the same after a ¼ turn? Give a reason for each answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: After a ½ turn: yes, the design looks the same. The top-left red cell rotates to the bottom-right position (which is also red), and the top-right blue cell rotates to the bottom-left position (which is also blue), so every cell maps to a cell of the same colour. After a ¼ turn: no, the design does not look the same. The top-left red cell rotates to the top-right position, which is blue — so the colours do not match after a quarter-turn.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Rotate the 2×2 grid 90° and 180° and check whether each coloured cell lands on a cell of the same colour.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student colour a drawn 2×2 grid, cut it out, and physically rotate it to compare; stretch: ask the student to find a two-colour arrangement of the 2×2 grid that looks the same after every ¼ turn.

exercise.description: Does the 2-colour 2×2 square design look the same after ½ turn? Does it look the same after ¼ turn?

items.section_title: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
items.prompt: A wooden printing block is carved in the shape of a fish facing right. When it is pressed onto paper, which direction does the fish in the print face? Explain why using the idea of reflection symmetry.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The fish in the print faces left. When the block is pressed face-down onto paper and lifted, the image is the mirror image of the block — it is flipped left-to-right. This is exactly what happens with reflection symmetry across a vertical axis: right becomes left and left becomes right.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Pressing a block face-down reverses it left-to-right, just as a mirror reflects a shape — the print is the reflection of the block.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student press a thumb dipped in ink onto paper and compare the thumb's orientation with the print; stretch: ask the student what would change if the block were pressed twice, the second time rotated ½ turn.

exercise.description: Match each wooden block (i–v) to its correct print (a–e) by drawing a line. One is done for you.

items.section_title: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
items.prompt: A border design repeats the same shape every ½ turn. How many times does the design look exactly the same during one full turn?

options.label: B
options.text: It never looks the same before a full turn.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Twice. A design that looks the same every ½ turn matches at the ½-turn position and again at the full-turn position — that is two times in one complete rotation (the full turn is always counted as one of the matching positions in the chapter's treatment).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the fractional turns at which the design matches within one full rotation, including the full turn itself.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be counting only the intermediate matching position (½ turn) and forgetting the full turn.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confusing this with a ¼-turn design, which matches four times.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not recognised that ½-turn symmetry means the design matches before completing the full turn.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student rotate a simple design step by step and mark each position where it matches; stretch: ask how many times a design with ¼-turn symmetry looks the same in a full turn.

exercise.description: Design B: fill in 'The design B looks the same after every __ turn. This design has __ symmetry.'
